claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained load in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy nanoscale multilayers is governed by the nature of the layer interfaces.
Greater interface disorder and incoherence accelerate creep deformation.
Compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and possible short-range order increase interface disorder or incoherence.
Interface disorder and incoherence promote heterogeneous dislocation nucleation and channeling.
The standard deposition route produces relatively coherent interfaces in the starting FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayer.
Controlled thermal annealing can reduce interface coherence while preserving the nanoscale multilayer architecture.
Interface disorder or coherence controls the density of dislocation-nucleation sites at layer boundaries.
Interface disorder or coherence controls the ease of dislocation nucleation at layer boundaries.
Loss of interface coherence increases local stress concentrations.
Less-coherent interfaces provide preferential sites for dislocation nucleation.
Dislocations nucleated at less-coherent interfaces propagate more readily under sustained stress.
More readily propagating dislocations produce progressive plastic deformation.
Severe lattice distortions inherent to high-entropy alloys accentuate localized deformation when interfaces are less coherent.
Under otherwise identical loading conditions, the annealed specimen with reduced interface coherence will have a higher creep strain rate than the coherent-interface baseline.
Under otherwise identical loading conditions, the annealed specimen will accumulate more creep strain than the coherent-interface baseline.
Confined layer slip may also contribute to deformation.
